Plotting is one of the places where `np` becomes especially useful, because the fitted object often carries much more than a point estimate. The package also supports asymptotic and bootstrap-based uncertainty summaries, but those come with real computational cost.

If you want a minimal downloadable script for this route, start with [np_plotting_quickstart.R](www/np_npRmpi/np_plotting_quickstart.R).

::: {.callout-note}
## Current plotting interface

This page reflects the `npRmpi` `0.80-1` and `np` `0.80-1` releases, both
available on CRAN.

- use `errors`, `bootstrap`, `band`, `alpha`, and `B` for the main interval controls
- use dotted names such as `data.rug`, `data.overlay`, `common.scale`, and `coef.index`
- use `np_boot_control()`, `np_grid_control()`, and `np_render_control()` only for the remaining detailed control groups

The former underscore spellings of public plot controls are retired rather
than silently translated. For example, use `data.rug`, not `data_rug`, and
`render.control`, not `render_control`.

In estimator calls, uncertainty is requested with `se = TRUE`; predictions use
`se.fit = TRUE`, and `gradients(object, se = TRUE)` requests gradient standard
errors. Plot methods deliberately retain the method-valued control
`errors = "asymptotic"` or `errors = "bootstrap"`.

Older plotting code that uses `plot.errors.*` names should translate those
controls to the public arguments above.

Fitted objects and their bandwidth objects now retain the prepared sample used
for plotting, including subset and missing-data decisions. Copula grid size is
the exception to ordinary post-fit grid adjustment: set `neval` or supply `u`
when constructing `npcopula()`, because `plot.npcopula()` rejects `neval`.
:::

## A simple fitted-curve plot

Start with the smallest possible case.

```r
## Load the package and a simple example dataset
library(np)
data(cps71, package = "np")

## Fit a local-linear model, then ask plot() for bootstrap error bounds
model.ll <- npreg(logwage ~ age, regtype = "ll", data = cps71)
plot(model.ll,
  errors = "bootstrap",
  bootstrap = "inid",
  band = "all")
```

## Asymptotic intervals

For many users, asymptotic intervals are the first reasonable uncertainty summary because they are much lighter than full bootstrap procedures.

```r
## Add asymptotic error bounds to the same fitted object
plot(model.ll, errors = "asymptotic")
```

## Gradients

For derivative views, request gradients in the plot call.

```r
## Request derivative plots from the same fitted object
plot(model.ll, gradients = TRUE)
```

And again with asymptotic intervals:

```r
## Combine derivative plots with asymptotic error bounds
plot(model.ll, gradients = TRUE, errors = "asymptotic")
```

## Bootstrap intervals

Bootstrap-based intervals are often appealing because they are less tied to asymptotic formulas, but they can be slow.

```r
## Use the bootstrap route when you want simulation-based intervals
plot(model.ll, errors = "bootstrap")
```

Current `np` and `npRmpi` releases also support bias-corrected bootstrap
centering on the supported fixed-bandwidth plot families. Unsupported routes
fail explicitly rather than silently drawing a different interval.

For fixed-bandwidth conditional density/distribution and gradient plots, the
bias-corrected center uses a mixed-data pilot matched to the selected response
and conditioning kernels and retains the selected LC/LL/LP estimator. These
explicitly requested centers can differ from earlier releases; ordinary fitted
values and estimate-centered bootstrap variability draws are unchanged.

Current bootstrap implementations avoid unnecessary public-facing quadratic
storage on ordinary default grids. The default evaluation grids for
single-index, conditional-mode, and partially-linear plots grow linearly with
the training sample size; an explicit request such as `neval = ntrain` remains
under user control and can still be substantially heavier. Fixed
local-polynomial plot bootstraps use a shared count-compressed, bounded-ridge
response solver across the supported regression and conditional families.
Long bootstrap plots retain one call-scoped elapsed clock and provide an
approximate overall ETA across scheduled targets.

Fixed and geometric plot-bootstrap draws are replication ordered, so a fixed
seed no longer depends on bootstrap chunk size or the number of MPI workers.
That stronger reproducibility contract can change seeded bands relative to an
older package version.

```r
## Ask supported bootstrap plots to use bias-corrected centers
plot(model.ll,
  errors = "bootstrap",
  center = "bias-corrected")
```

For serious work, this is exactly the sort of route where separating bandwidth selection from later estimation and plotting is especially worthwhile.

## Interactive `rgl` rendering and rugs

When `rgl` is installed, plot methods can also render interactive 3D surfaces
via `renderer = "rgl"`. That gives you a manipulable display: drag with the
mouse to rotate and use the scroll wheel to zoom. The same plotting surface now
also supports 1D/2D rugs and data-overlay controls via the direct
`data.rug` and `data.overlay` arguments.

The current widget uses a high-DPI-aware canvas and construction-aware interval
legends while preserving ordinary `rgl.*` overrides.

These are best viewed in RStudio, where the interactive surface appears in the
Viewer pane rather than the Plot pane.

If you want a minimal runnable script for this route, use
[np_rgl_quickstart.R](www/np_npRmpi/np_rgl_quickstart.R).

```r
## Fit a small bivariate model, then draw it with the interactive renderer
library(np)
data(wage1, package = "np")

fit_rgl <- npreg(lwage ~ educ + exper,
  regtype = "ll",
  data = wage1)

plot(fit_rgl,
  view = "fixed",
  renderer = "rgl",
  errors = "asymptotic",
  data.overlay = FALSE,
  data.rug = TRUE)
```

The same renderer is also useful for conditional density/distribution surfaces
when you want to inspect shape changes interactively rather than through a fixed
static viewpoint.

## Partial regression plots

For multivariate models, `plot()` typically constructs partial regression plots: one covariate varies while the others are held fixed at representative values such as medians or modes.

That is why these plots are often smoother and easier to read than simply plotting raw data against one regressor at a time in a multivariate setting.

## A multivariate example

```r
## Build a multivariate fit, then let plot() create the partial views
library(np)
data(wage1, package = "np")

fit_multi <- npreg(lwage ~ female + married + educ + exper + tenure,
  regtype = "ll",
  data = wage1)

plot(fit_multi, errors = "bootstrap")
```

This is a high-value visualization, but it is not a cheap one.

## Prediction

Once a model is fitted, prediction is straightforward. Supply new explanatory data via `newdata`.

```r
## Predict on a small evaluation grid
cps_eval <- data.frame(age = seq(10, 70, by = 10))
predict(model.ll, newdata = cps_eval)
```

If you request `se.fit = TRUE`, the prediction route will also return asymptotic standard errors where supported.

## A practical warning about runtime

Plotting can trigger real computation, especially when:

- gradients are requested,
- asymptotic errors are recovered,
- bootstrap intervals are requested,
- the model itself is multivariate or expensive.

So if a plot does not appear instantly, that does not necessarily mean anything is wrong.

## One common source of confusion

The values returned by `gradients(fit)` are not the same object as the smooth partial-regression plots generated by `plot(fit, gradients = TRUE)` in multivariate settings. The plot method is constructing an evaluation path that is easier to interpret visually, while `gradients(fit)` returns derivative information tied to the model object’s evaluation structure.
